steps.title: Esophagus
steps.instruction: Trace the esophagus down from the mouth.

note.text: After you chew and swallow, muscles in the esophagus squeeze food down to the stomach in waves.
The stomach churns food and mixes it with acid and enzymes that start breaking it down.
The liver makes bile, which helps break fats into tiny droplets so they can be digested.

steps.title: Pancreas
steps.instruction: Trace the pancreas below the stomach.

note.text: The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and sends them into the small intestine.

steps.title: Small intestine
steps.instruction: Trace the long, winding small intestine.

note.text: About 3 m long, the small intestine is where most digestion and almost all absorption of nutrients happen.
note.remember: Small intestine: nutrients into the blood.

steps.title: Large intestine
steps.instruction: Trace the large intestine around the outside, down to the rectum.

note.text: The large intestine absorbs most of the leftover water, then the waste leaves through the rectum.

steps.title: Food's path
steps.instruction: Tap the places food passes through, in order.
steps.why: Food goes down the esophagus to the stomach, then the small intestine absorbs nutrients and the large intestine absorbs water.
steps.hint: The liver and pancreas help, but food doesn't pass through them.

steps.title: Name the organs
steps.instruction: Pick the name for each numbered organ.

mistakes.Stomach: The stomach is the J-shaped bag above. This organ below it is the pancreas.

mistakes.Large intestine: The large intestine frames the outside. This long winding tube is the small intestine.

steps.title: Systems working together
steps.question: Nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. How do they reach your muscles?

options.text: They pass into the blood, and the circulatory system carries them
options.feedback: Yes. The digestive system breaks food down; the circulatory system delivers it to every cell.

options.text: They travel down the large intestine
options.feedback: That carries waste out. Nutrients enter the blood in the small intestine.
Muscles get nutrients from the blood, which picks them up in the small intestine.
The lungs handle gases. Nutrients travel in the blood.

steps.title: Why so long?
steps.question: Why is it useful that the small intestine is so long?

options.text: It gives lots of surface for absorbing nutrients
options.feedback: Right. Its great length, plus folds inside, gives a huge surface for nutrients to pass into the blood.
Food passes through in hours. The length gives more surface for absorption.
That's mostly the large intestine. The small intestine absorbs nutrients.
The liver makes bile. The length gives more surface for absorbing nutrients.
